The solana.com page says to load 'the v11.0.0 program from devnet' to run the examples. Mainnet deployment is still unverified.
facts.as_of: main branch fetched 2026-10-06; source is newer than the docs page
facts.design_relevance: The extension list keeps growing, so the gate has to reject by default any extension type it does not recognise or cannot parse.
facts.original_claim: On the token-2022 main branch, the ExtensionType enum in interface/src/extension/mod.rs has one more variant after PausableAccount: PermissionedBurn ('Tokens burning requires approval from authority'). It also adds AuthorityType::PermissionedBurn. The official docs list (TH-04) does not include it yet. I could not verify whether it is deployed to the mainnet Token-2022 program.
facts.note: The source facts are right, but 'the official docs do not include it yet' is wrong: two official docs pages describe it. The docs state it is on devnet as v11.0.0 and say nothing about mainnet.

facts.claim: The Token-2022 docs say the permanent delegate 'has unlimited delegate privileges over any account for that mint, meaning that it can burn or transfer any amount'. In source, AuthorityType::PermanentDelegate is described as 'Authority to transfer or burn any tokens for a mint'.
facts.design_relevance: If a mint has a non-null permanent delegate, the bot should hard reject it, because the delegate can take or burn the bot's tokens at any time.
facts.note: Both quotes match verbatim.

facts.claim: A Token-2022 transfer fee is set in basis points up to MAX_FEE_BASIS_POINTS = 10,000 (100%), with a maximum_fee: u64 cap. The transfer fee authority can change it with SetTransferFee. The processor schedules a new fee to start at current epoch + 2, with the comment 'set two epochs ahead to avoid rug pulls at the end of an epoch'.
facts.design_relevance: Reject tokens with a non-zero fee or a live fee authority, because the fee can be raised to 100% with two epochs' notice. If a fee is ever allowed, it must be added to the cost model and checked against newer_transfer_fee.
facts.note: MAX_FEE_BASIS_POINTS is 10_000, maximum_fee is a U64 and SetTransferFee exists. The processor has 'set two epochs ahead to avoid rug pulls at the end of an epoch' and epoch.saturating_add(2).

facts.claim: With TransferHook, Token-2022 makes a CPI into the hook program after all other transfer logic. In processor.rs the call is Execute{...}.invoke()?, so an error from the hook fails the transfer. The hook program id can be changed later by the transfer hook authority with the Update instruction (AuthorityType::TransferHookProgramId).
facts.design_relevance: A transfer hook can block sells whenever it wants (a programmable honeypot), and the hook program can be swapped later. Hard reject any mint whose hook program id is non-null.
facts.note: The docs say 'This call happens after all other transfer logic'. The processor (now pinocchio-based) calls Execute{...}.invoke()? at the end of the transfer. The Update instruction changes the hook program id, and AuthorityType::TransferHookProgramId exists.

facts.claim: The DefaultAccountState extension can 'force all new token accounts to be frozen', so 'users must eventually interact with some service to unfreeze their account'. GoPlus reports this as default_account_state ('2' = Frozen) plus a default_account_state_upgradable flag.
facts.design_relevance: Reject a default state of Frozen, and also reject when the default-state authority could switch new accounts to Frozen.
facts.note: Both quotes match. GoPlus documents default_account_state with "2" for Frozen, and a default_account_state_upgradable object.

facts.claim: With the Pausable extension, the mint's pause authority can pause and resume minting, burning and transferring. The docs say 'the program aborts all transfers, mints, and burns when the paused flag is flipped'.
facts.design_relevance: A pause authority can stop every sell, so Pausable mints should be a hard reject.
facts.note: Pause and Resume cover 'minting, burning, and transferring'. The docs text reads 'aborts all tranfers, mints, and burns when the paused flag is flipped' (typo in the original).

facts.topic: Mint close authority (vendor description conflicts with source)
facts.claim: In the Token-2022 processor, closing a mint returns TokenError::MintHasSupply ('Mint has non-zero supply. Burn all tokens before closing the mint') unless supply == 0. This conflicts with GoPlus's description of its 'closable' field: 'If the programme is closed, all the assets would be eliminated.'
facts.design_relevance: Vendor field descriptions can be wrong. Base risk rules on program source, and use vendor flags only as secondary signals. MintCloseAuthority on its own is low risk, but combined with PermanentDelegate (burn everything, then close) it is dangerous.
facts.note: The processor returns MintHasSupply when supply != 0, and the error text matches. The GoPlus 'closable' description is verbatim, so the conflict is real.

facts.claim: The Token-2022 ScaledUiAmount extension stores an authority that 'can set the scaling amount and authority', a multiplier applied to raw amounts, and a new_multiplier that takes effect at new_multiplier_effective_timestamp. UI amounts are computed as raw amount times multiplier.
facts.design_relevance: The authority can change UI amounts and any prices derived from them. The bot should do accounting in raw base units only, and reject or flag mints that have ScaledUiAmount or InterestBearingConfig.
facts.note: The authority comment, multiplier, new_multiplier and new_multiplier_effective_timestamp all match. The scaled amount is amount * current_multiplier, with decimals applied separately.

facts.claim: The Metaplex Token Metadata account (program metaqbxxUerdq28cj1RbAWkYQm3ybzjb6a8bt518x1s) contains update_authority: Pubkey, mint, data (name/symbol/uri, etc.), primary_sale_happened and is_mutable: bool, with the comment 'Whether or not the data struct is mutable, default is not'.
facts.design_relevance: Treat mutable metadata as a soft risk: established tokens such as BONK also have it (TH-21). Never identify a token by name, symbol or image; use only the mint address.
facts.note: declare_id metaqbxx... matches, and so do the struct fields and the is_mutable comment.

facts.topic: Token-2022 on-mint metadata and pointer spoofing
facts.claim: In Token-2022, TokenMetadata has update_authority: MaybeNull, and its mint field is 'used to counter spoofing to be sure that metadata belongs to a particular mint'. MetadataPointer has an authority that 'can set the metadata address' and a metadata_address.
facts.design_relevance: The bot should check TokenMetadata.mint == mint, and note whether the pointer authority or the update authority is still live, because either can repoint or rewrite the metadata.
facts.note: The update_authority MaybeNull type, the anti-spoofing mint comment, and the MetadataPointer authority and metadata_address fields all match.

facts.claim: In the same 2026 study, the authors found 1,030 rug tokens whose names closely imitate well-known tokens or brands (e.g., 'USDTea', 'USDTf', 'TIKTOK'), plus tokens whose symbols copy mainstream symbols (e.g., USDT, SOLANA) under unrelated names. Of the 76,469 rug tokens, only 19.0% disclose an X account and 14.3% a website.
facts.design_relevance: Signals from names or social links are weak. The dashboard should always show the mint address and the bot should only ever key on mints. Off-chain presence alone is not a safety signal.
facts.note: The paper gives 1,030 look-alike names (e.g., USDTea, USDTf, TIKTOK), and 14,552 (19.0%) X accounts and 10,957 (14.3%) websites among the 76,469 tokens.

facts.claim: Pump.fun's create_v2 instruction creates a new Token-2022 mint (program TokenzQdBNbLqP5VEhdkAS6EPFLC1PHnBqCXEpPxuEb) with decimals = 6, the metadata pointer set to the mint itself, and mint_authority set to a Pump PDA (seeds [b"mint-authority"]). Creator-chosen name is limited to 32 characters, symbol to 13 and URI to 200. RugCheck reports pulled on 2026-10-06 for recent '...pump' mints showed tokenProgram = TokenzQdBNbLqP5VEhdkAS6EPFLC1PHnBqCXEpPxuEb.
facts.design_relevance: The bot must parse Token-2022 extensions for ordinary pump.fun coins, and it has to tell launchpad-PDA authorities apart from creator-held ones. I did not verify whether the mint authority is revoked after creation.
facts.note: The doc confirms decimals 6, the metadata pointer set to the mint, the Pump PDA [b"mint-authority"], and limits of 32/13/200. The rugs/ticker endpoint does not return tokenProgram. Per-token reports and new_tokens do show the Token-2022 program for '...pump' mints. See the missed item on authorities after creation.

facts.claim: The Pump program docs state: 'When the coin hits a certain market cap the liquidity from the bonding curve is migrated to PumpSwap... The LP tokens received from the PumpSwap pool are then burnt.' Anyone can call migrate, it is idempotent, and pools created by migrate use canonical pool index 0. The program address is 6EF8rrecthR5Dkzon8Nwu78hRvfCKubJ14M5uBEwF6P.
facts.design_relevance: The canonical migrated pool cannot be drained by an LP withdrawal, so the main risk for these tokens is insiders dumping, not a liquidity pull.
facts.note: The migration and LP-burn quote, the permissionless idempotent migrate, CANONONICAL_POOL_INDEX == 0 (typo in the original) and the 6EF8... address on mainnet and devnet all match.

facts.topic: PumpSwap non-canonical pools / LP supply accounting
facts.claim: PumpSwap create_pool(index, creator, baseMint, quoteMint, baseIn, quoteIn) lets the same creator open several pools for one pair. The creator receives lpMint tokens that 'can be later used to withdraw liquidity'. Pool::lp_supply is 'the total supply of the lp_mint without burns and lock-ups', so it does not show user burns.
facts.design_relevance: LP burn/lock status must be checked for each pool. Trade only in pools whose LP is verified burned or locked (e.g., canonical index 0), and calculate the burned share from the LP mint's actual supply and holders, not from Pool::lp_supply.
facts.note: The create_pool signature, the index allowing multiple pools per creator and pair, the lpMint 'can be later used to withdraw' line and the lp_supply 'without burns and lock-ups' line all match.

facts.claim: PumpSwap's GlobalConfig admin can call disable(admin, disable_create_pool, disable_deposit, disable_withdraw, disable_buy, disable_sell) to 'globally disable any Pump Swap operation', and can change LP and protocol fees with update_fee_config.
facts.design_relevance: A venue can halt sells or change fees. The bot needs a venue-health circuit breaker and should treat a disabled-sell state as a stop condition, not as a bug to retry.
facts.note: The disable() signature and update_fee_config match. Caveats: the same README also says GlobalConfig.disable_flags is 'Currently, it is not used', which conflicts. The current IDL's update_fee_config also takes coin_creator_fee_basis_points and admin_set_coin_creator_authority, so the admin can change more fees than LP and protocol fees.

facts.claim: Raydium Burn & Earn puts CPMM LP tokens or CLMM position NFTs into a program-owned escrow. They are not destroyed, and the liquidity 'can never be withdrawn'. Fees go to whoever holds a transferable Fee Key NFT. It supports CPMM and CLMM (full-range recommended) but not AMM v4, and there is no partial lock.
facts.design_relevance: An LP-safety check must recognise three states: burned, escrow-locked by a known program, and unlocked. AMM v4 pools cannot use Burn & Earn, so their LP has to be checked for burning or another locker.
facts.note: The page says LP is locked in a program-owned escrow and not destroyed, 'can never be withdrawn', with a transferable Fee Key NFT. Its table shows CPMM Yes, CLMM full-range only (recommended), AMM v4 Not supported. It also says 'There is no partial lock'.

facts.claim: In the RugCheck swagger, GET /v1/tokens/{id}/report and GET /v1/tokens/{id}/report/summary have no security requirement. Bulk report/summary, lockers, verify and vote endpoints need an 'Authorization' JWT API key, and the 'refresh' parameter is 'paid API keys only'. The summary returns score, score_normalised, risks[name, level, description, score, value], lpLockedPct and tokenProgram. An unauthenticated call on 2026-10-06 returned the header x-rate-limit-limit: 15; the window is not documented.
facts.design_relevance: Free use is possible but tightly rate-limited, and the window is unknown. Use RugCheck as a cached second opinion after the bot's own on-chain gate, not inside the hot path.
facts.note: In the swagger, the GET report and summary endpoints have no security requirement, while bulk, lockers, verify and POST vote need ApiKeyAuth (Authorization JWT). refresh is 'paid API keys only'. The TokenCheckSummary fields match. Every response I received also had x-rate-limit-limit: 15, and the window is still undocumented. GET /votes needs no auth.

facts.topic: RugCheck observed risk names and report fields
facts.claim: Live RugCheck reports fetched 2026-10-06 included these fields: mintAuthority, freezeAuthority, token_extensions, tokenMeta.mutable/updateAuthority, topHolders[pct], insiderNetworks, graphInsidersDetected, markets, lockers, transferFee, rugged and creatorBalance. Observed risk names were 'Freeze Authority still enabled' (danger, score 25000), 'Single holder ownership' (danger), 'Low Liquidity' (danger), 'High holder concentration' ('top 10 users hold more than 50%', warn), 'High holder correlation' (warn), 'Mutable metadata' (warn, score 100) and 'Missing file metadata' (warn). BONK showed graphInsidersDetected = 48 and the 'Mutable metadata' warning.
facts.as_of: 2026-10-06 (live API output; the field set is not in the swagger schema)
facts.design_relevance: These are useful labels for insider/cluster and concentration checks. Because the schema is undocumented, parse defensively and treat a missing field as unknown, never as safe.
facts.note: All listed fields appear. BONK has graphInsidersDetected=48 and 'Mutable metadata' (warn, 100). I observed 'Freeze Authority still enabled' (danger, 25000), 'Single holder ownership' and 'Low Liquidity'. I did not see 'High holder concentration', 'High holder correlation' or 'Missing file metadata' in my samples. I did see other names: 'Top 10 holders high ownership' (>70%, danger), 'High ownership' (>80%, danger), 'Mint Authority still enabled' and 'Creator history of rugged tokens'.

facts.topic: RugCheck live rug statistics (vendor, low quality)
facts.claim: RugCheck GET /v1/stats/analytics (window '7d', fetched 2026-10-06) reported tokensLaunched pump_fun 373,917 and rugPullCount pump_fun 35,272 (about 9.4%); meteora_dbc 17,550/9,037; meteora_damm_v2 26,627/5,320; raydium_launchlab 13,779/542. The same response gave rugMarketCapUSD = 930,647,322,291,096,800, which is implausible, and the definition of 'rug' is not documented.
facts.design_relevance: This shows how many tokens launch each week (about 374k a week on pump.fun) and that vendor 'rug' counts are noisy. Do not use them as a base rate without a stated definition.
facts.note: My later fetch the same day returned window '7d' with pump_fun 374,812/35,342 (9.4%), meteora_dbc 18,780/9,044, meteora_damm_v2 26,668/5,319, raydium_launchlab 13,770/541 and rugMarketCapUSD ~9.3e17. The figures are rolling, but the magnitudes and the implausible market cap reproduce. No definition of 'rug' is documented.

facts.claim: GoPlus documents GET https://api.gopluslabs.io/api/v1/solana/token_security?contract_addresses=..., labelled 'Token Security API for Solana (Beta)', with an optional 'Authorization: Bearer' header. Result fields: balance_mutable_authority, closable, creators, default_account_state, default_account_state_upgradable, dex (burn_percent, tvl, fee_rate, open_time, type...), freezable, holders (top 10), lp_holders, metadata, metadata_mutable, mintable, none_transferable, transfer_fee, transfer_fee_upgradable, transfer_hook, transfer_hook_upgradable and trusted_token.
facts.design_relevance: This is the vendor field set that maps most closely to Token-2022 trap extensions, but it is still labelled Beta. Use it as a cross-check against the bot's own parsing.
facts.note: The docs are labelled '(Beta)', updatedAt 2026-08-20. contract_addresses is required and the Authorization Bearer header is not marked required. The result field list matches.

facts.claim: GoPlus's pricing page lists a Free Version at 150K API CU/month, 30k CU/day and 150 CU/min. Paid packages are Test $199/month (6M CU), Beginner $399, Growth $799, Pro $1,899 and Ultra $3,499. The table says batch calls are 'Not enabled' on Free and enabled from Test upwards, but the FAQ on the same page says batch is only for Pro, Ultra or Enterprise. CU cost per Solana call is not stated.
facts.design_relevance: The free tier may cover low-volume checks. Paid tiers are 20% or more of the bankroll each month and cannot be justified.
facts.note: The table shows Free 150K CU/month, 30k/day, 150/min, then $199/399/799/1,899/3,499. The batch row says 'Not enabled' on Free and Enabled from Test upwards, while the FAQ says batch is only for Pro, Ultra or Enterprise. That contradiction is real.

facts.topic: Birdeye token security endpoint and cost
facts.claim: Birdeye GET https://public-api.birdeye.so/defi/token_security (header x-chain, default solana; X-API-KEY required) costs 30 CU per request and is listed for Lite, Starter, Premium, Business and Enterprise, but not the free Standard package. Pricing: Standard $0 (30,000 CU, 1 rps), Lite $39/month (2.5M CU, 15 rps, $23 per extra 1M CU), Starter $99, Premium $199. Solana response fields include creatorPercentage, metaplexUpdateAuthority, mutableMetadata, top10HolderPercent, freezeAuthority/freezeable, transferFeeEnable/transferFeeData, isToken2022, nonTransferable, lockInfo, fakeToken, isTrueToken, preMarketHolder and jupStrictList.
facts.design_relevance: The cheapest tier with access is $39/month, about 47% a year of a $1k bankroll, for roughly 83k security calls a month. The documented Solana example has no permanent-delegate, transfer-hook or pausable fields, so it does not replace the bot's own extension parsing.
facts.note: The endpoint costs 30 CU. The access table (effective 26-Nov-2025) has no Standard checkmark. Pricing is Standard $0/30k/1rps and Lite $39/2.5M/15rps/$23 per extra 1M. The Solana example fields match, with no permanent-delegate, hook or pausable fields; transferPausable appears only in the EVM example.

facts.claim: The Jupiter Tokens API v2 (https://api.jup.ag/tokens/v2/..., x-api-key required) returns an audit object whose fields are present only when relevant: isSus, mintAuthorityDisabled, freezeAuthorityDisabled, topHoldersPercentage, devBalancePercentage and devMints. It also returns organicScore (0-100) with organicScoreLabel, isVerified and tags, plus stats windows with organic buy/sell volume.
facts.design_relevance: This is an extra safety and wash-volume signal. Pricing and limits belong to the EX researcher. Because the fields are conditional, a missing audit field must count as unknown.
facts.note: The guide says x-api-key is required. The audit fields are 'all fields conditional', with isSus 'only present when true'. organicScore 0-100 with a label, isVerified, and stats windows with buyOrganicVolume/sellOrganicVolume are all present.

facts.claim: The Agave account-decoder (jsonParsed encoding) maps every Token-2022 ExtensionType to a UI type, including PermanentDelegate, TransferHook, DefaultAccountState, Pausable, ScaledUiAmount and PermissionedBurn. Extensions it cannot parse come back as UiExtension::UnparseableExtension.
facts.as_of: master branch fetched 2026-10-06; RPC providers may run older versions
facts.design_relevance: A free, vendor-independent gate is possible: getAccountInfo(jsonParsed) on the mint, with any unparseable or unknown extension treated as a reject.
facts.note: The match covers all variants including PermissionedBurn, with .unwrap_or(UiExtension::UnparseableExtension). Deployed RPC versions may lag behind master.

facts.topic: Rug base rate: academic, non-pump.fun DEX tokens (2025)
facts.claim: arXiv 2603.24625 (Chen et al., 7 authors; v2 31 May 2026) applied its pipeline to 100,063 tokens newly issued on Orca, Raydium and Meteora between 2025-01-01 and 2025-06-30. It labelled 76,469 (~76.4%) as rug-pull candidates: 60,402 Pump-and-Dump, 15,606 Liquidity Withdrawal and 461 Freeze Authority Abuse. A 382-sample audit gave a 0.26% false-positive rate. The paper excludes 'Pump.fun-only tokens that never establish liquidity pools', but KEEPS Pump.fun-originated tokens that go on to create pools. Labels use a 24-hour observation window. In a 100-token sample of non-rug labels, 9 were missed rugs that unfolded over 3-7 days, so the rate is a lower bound.
facts.design_relevance: Under a published, audited definition, most new Solana DEX tokens are scams. Strategy evaluation should assume most tokens go to roughly zero, and survivorship bias in backtests is a serious risk.
facts.original_claim: arXiv 2603.24625 ('From Hype to Collapse: Investigating Rug Pull Scams on Solana', Chen et al., v2 2026-05-31) looked at 100,063 tokens newly issued on Orca, Raydium and Meteora between 2025-01-01 and 2025-06-30. Its pipeline labelled 76,469 (about 76.4%) as rug-pull candidates: 60,402 Pump-and-Dump, 15,606 Liquidity Withdrawal and 461 Freeze Authority Abuse. A manual audit of 382 sampled tokens gave a 0.26% false-positive rate. Pump.fun bonding-curve tokens were excluded from scope.
facts.note: All numbers match. 'Pump.fun bonding-curve tokens were excluded' overstates it: migrated pump.fun tokens are in the dataset, and many of the paper's examples have '...pump' mints. The 24-hour window and the ~9% miss rate were omitted.

facts.claim: In the same paper, Table IV gives an overall median rug lifespan (creation to first fraud-related profit-taking) of 0.024618 days (about 35 minutes), P25 0.008681 days and P75 0.064641 days (about 93 minutes); the Pump-and-Dump median is 0.022083 days (about 32 minutes). The paper estimates at least $151M in direct losses across 7,322 profiting addresses and finds 78 syndicates with a median of 36 members. The text says freeze-abuse median lifecycles are under one hour, but Table IV shows a freeze-abuse median of 0.483 days, so the paper is internally inconsistent on that point.
facts.design_relevance: Exits and time stops need to work on a scale of minutes, and token re-checks must be cheap enough to run often. Syndicate structure supports graph and funding-link checks.
facts.note: The paper defines lifecycle as 'creation and the first confirmed fraud-related profit-taking transaction'. Table IV values match, and freeze abuse shows a median of 0.483275 days against text saying 'less than one hour', so the inconsistency is real. The paper reports $151M, 7,322 addresses and 78 groups with members ranging 1-169 and a median of 36. Elsewhere it says 16 of the 78 are single scammers.

facts.topic: Rug base rate: pump.fun (vendor, loose definition)
facts.claim: Solidus Labs' '2025 Rug Pull Report' (May 2025) states that '98.6% of tokens on Pump.fun collapse into worthless pump-and-dump schemes'. That figure covers more than 7 million tokens with at least 5 trades (Jan 2024 to Mar 2025), and a token is classified as such when its remaining liquidity falls below $1,000. On Raydium, about 93% (361,000 of 388,000) of pools showed 'soft rug pull' traits, defined as 90% or more of pool liquidity removed.
facts.design_relevance: The definition counts plain failure (liquidity under $1k) as fraud. Read it as a collapse rate, not a fraud rate. Either way, a random pump.fun token should be priced as near-certain to go to zero.
facts.note: Quote, 7M+ tokens with at least five trades, the <$1,000 liquidity threshold, and 388,000 pools with ~93% (printed as '361,00') and the 90% threshold all match. Caveats: the same page says 98.7% in its summary, and the method excludes tokens 'upgraded to Raydium'. It is vendor research.

facts.claim: SolRPDS (Alhaidari, Kalal, Palanisamy, Sural; ACM CODASPY 2025; arXiv 2504.07132) derives from 3.69 billion Solana transactions over 2021-2024. It contains 62,895 suspicious liquidity pools, and 22,195 tokens in the dataset show rug-pull patterns.
facts.design_relevance: This is a public, labelled dataset that can be used to test the bot's rug detector offline before paper trading.
facts.note: Authors, 3.69 billion transactions, 62,895 suspicious pools, 22,195 tokens and 2021-2024 all match. The listing comment says 'Accepted paper to appear in ... CODASPY 2025', and v1 is dated 6 Apr 2025.

facts.claim: Chainalysis (29 Jan 2025) reported that 3.59% of tokens launched in 2024 (74,037 of 2,063,519) showed patterns that may be linked to pump-and-dump schemes. The study covered only Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Base. Its criteria were: one address added liquidity and later removed at least 65%, worth at least $1,000; the pool is inactive; and the pool had more than 100 transactions.
facts.design_relevance: The 3.59% figure must not be applied to Solana. Rates range from about 3.6% to 98.6% depending on definition and chain, so the bot's own labelled data should set the base rate.
facts.note: The post is dated January 29 and reports 3.59%, 74,037 of 2,063,519, and three criteria: at least 65% removed worth $1,000 or more, an inactive pool, and over 100 transactions. The analysis discusses Ethereum, BNB and Base, and the page never mentions Solana.

facts.claim: Pine Analytics (21 Apr 2025, about one month of data from 15 Mar) found more than 15,000 SOL of realized profit from deployer-funded same-block sniping, across more than 15,000 launches, 4,600+ sniper wallets and 10,400+ deployers. 87% of snipes were profitable; over 55% of positions exited within 1 minute and about 85% within 5 minutes. Detection relied on buys in the same block as deployment plus direct SOL transfers between deployer and sniper.
facts.design_relevance: If buyers in the launch block were funded by the deployer, that is a strong bundled-launch red flag. Any bot buying in the first minutes is likely the exit liquidity for these insiders.
facts.note: The post is dated Apr 21 with data from March 15. It reports >15,000 SOL, 15,000+ launches, 4,600+ snipers, 10,400+ deployers, 87% profitable, >55% exited in under 1 minute and ~85% within 5 minutes. This is a Substack analytics post, so it is weak evidence.

facts.claim: arXiv 2607.02795 (single author, A. U. Kamat; v3 2026-08-03) analysed 1,578,333 buyer observations from 166,098 pump.fun launches over 13.4 days. It found 1,012 persistent wallet cohorts (2-12 wallets, 2,965 addresses) and a contamination-adjusted first-30-minute buyer-count lift of +16.1% (95% CI +13.0% to +19.4%). In 7.0% of 5,419 treated launches there were zero non-cohort buyers in the first 30 minutes.
facts.design_relevance: Early buyer counts can be inflated by coordinated rings. Buyer counts and holder growth should be adjusted for clusters before they feed any signal.
facts.note: The abstract matches: single author A. U. Kamat, v3 dated 3 Aug 2026, data from 2026-06-11 to 06-25. The abstract also says the SOL-inflow lift (+6.3%, CI -0.5% to +15.1%) is not distinguishable from zero, and that the placebo estimator is biased.

facts.claim: Bitquery (blog, analysis of 12 hours of Solana DEX data on 27-28 Apr 2026) found that one funder seeded at least 200 bots with exactly 0.5 SOL each in a 52-second burst on 2026-04-21, before the analysis window. In the 12-hour window the token OpenLie reported $532,461 of DEX volume from 233 wallets running 40,523 trades, averaging $13.14 per trade. 96% of the wallets both bought and sold, and the top 10 wash wallets had round-trip ratios of 0.95-1.00.
facts.design_relevance: Raw volume and trade counts cannot be trusted as signals. Before volume counts, apply wash filters: same-funder clustering, the share of wallets trading both sides, and round-trip ratios close to 1.
facts.original_claim: A Bitquery analysis (data 27-28 Apr 2026) found one funder seeding 200 bots with exactly 0.5 SOL each within 52 seconds. Those bots generated $532,461 of reported volume on one token in 12 hours. 96% of the wallets both bought and sold the token, and top wash wallets had buy/sell round-trip ratios of 0.95-1.00.
facts.note: The seeding happened on 21 Apr, not within the 27-28 Apr window, and the volume came from 233 wallets, not only the 200 seeded bots. It is a vendor blog.

facts.claim: GitHub advisory GHSA-jcxm-7wvp-g6p5 / CVE-2024-54134: @solana/web3.js versions 1.95.6 and 1.95.7 were malicious and available from 15:20 to 20:25 UTC on 3 Dec 2024. The patched version is 1.95.8. The code was designed to 'steal private key material and drain funds from dapps' that handle private keys directly. The advisory advises rotating any suspect authority keys, including multisigs, program authorities and server keypairs.
facts.design_relevance: A server-side bot that holds raw keys is exactly the affected profile. It needs exact version pins with lockfile integrity hashes, a delay before adopting new releases, and signing isolated from the general dependency tree.
facts.note: Fetched via WebFetch because curl got a 403. Versions 1.95.6 and 1.95.7, patched in 1.95.8, window 3:20pm-8:25pm UTC on 3 Dec 2024, CVE-2024-54134, published 4 Dec 2024. The key-rotation advice is quoted correctly.

facts.topic: Supply chain: malicious Solana-targeting npm packages
facts.claim: Socket reported three campaigns. (1) 2 Dec 2024: solana-systemprogram-utils@1.0.0 redirected about 2% of transfers (Math.random() < 0.02) to a hardcoded key. (2) 8 Jan 2025: @async-mutex/mutex, dexscreener, solana-transaction-toolkit and solana-stable-web-huks exfiltrated keys via Gmail SMTP. Only solana-transaction-toolkit and solana-stable-web-huks also drained wallets, taking 'up to 98%'. They were pulled in by GitHub repos moonshot-wif-hwan/pumpfun-bump-script-bot and Diveinprogramming/raydium-pumpfun-fastest-sniper-bot. (3) 24 Mar 2026: raydium-bs58, base-x-64, bs58-basic and base_xd targeted Solana base58 decode(), and ethersproject-wallet targeted Ethereum. All of them sent keys to a Telegram bot.
facts.design_relevance: Typosquats of common Solana helpers such as bs58, raydium-* and dexscreener are a recurring vector. Use a dependency allowlist with exact package names, and alert on outbound SMTP or Telegram traffic from the bot host.
facts.original_claim: Socket reported three Solana-targeting npm campaigns. (1) 2 Dec 2024: solana-systemprogram-utils@1.0.0 sent about 2% of transfers (Math.random() < 0.02) to a hardcoded attacker key. (2) 8 Jan 2025: @async-mutex/mutex, dexscreener, solana-transaction-toolkit and solana-stable-web-huks exfiltrated private keys via Gmail SMTP, two of them auto-transferring 98% of wallet funds, and they were imported by GitHub repos 'moonshot-wif-hwan' and 'Diveinprogramming'. (3) 24 Mar 2026: raydium-bs58, base-x-64 and bs58-basic exfiltrated keys to a Telegram bot.
facts.note: Fetched via WebFetch (curl 403). 'moonshot-wif-hwan' and 'Diveinprogramming' are GitHub accounts, not repo names. The drain was 'up to 98%'. The third campaign also included base_xd. These are vendor blogs.

facts.claim: Socket (24 May 2026) reported 'TrapDoor': 'more than 34 malicious packages and 384+ related versions and artifacts' across npm, PyPI and crates.io. It stole SSH keys, Sui/Solana/Aptos wallet data, AWS and GitHub credentials, browser profiles, environment variables and API keys. It ran via npm postinstall (trap-core.js), crates.io build.rs and PyPI import-time remote JS execution. The earliest upload was PyPI eth-security-auditor@0.1.0 on 22 May 2026 at 20:20:18 UTC.
facts.design_relevance: Install-time and build-time code execution reaches environment variables and key files. Builds should happen in a sandbox with no secrets, install scripts should be disabled, and keys must never sit in environment variables on a build host.
facts.original_claim: Socket (24 May 2026) reported 'TrapDoor': 34 malicious packages with 384+ versions or artifacts across npm, PyPI and crates.io. It stole SSH keys, Sui/Solana/Aptos wallet data, AWS credentials, GitHub tokens, environment variables and API keys. It ran through npm postinstall hooks, crates.io build.rs scripts and PyPI import-time payloads. The earliest package was uploaded on 22 May 2026 at 20:20:18 UTC.
facts.note: Socket says 'more than 34', not exactly 34. Everything else matches. Fetched via WebFetch; it is a vendor blog.

facts.topic: Supply chain: Sept 2025 npm maintainer compromise
facts.claim: On 8 Sep 2025 a maintainer compromised through a phishing email had packages republished with a crypto-stealer, including debug@4.4.2, chalk@5.6.1 and color@5.0.1. duckdb@1.3.3, along with @duckdb/node-api@1.3.3, @duckdb/node-bindings@1.3.3 and @duckdb/duckdb-wasm@1.29.2, came from a SECOND compromised account by the same actor, added in Semgrep's 9 Sep update. Semgrep says the payload re-routes Bitcoin, Solana, Ethereum and other transactions to attacker addresses by rewriting HTTP responses.
facts.design_relevance: Even ubiquitous non-crypto transitive dependencies can be weaponised. The dashboard frontend must never handle signing, and the transaction recipient must be checked after construction in a minimal signer.
facts.original_claim: On 8 Sep 2025 a phished npm maintainer's packages were republished with a crypto-stealer, including debug@4.4.2, chalk@5.6.1, color@5.0.1 and duckdb@1.3.3. Semgrep says the payload rerouted Bitcoin, Solana and Ethereum transactions to attacker addresses.
facts.note: duckdb was not part of the same phished maintainer's packages. The payload works by rewriting HTTP responses, so it is browser/web-facing, which matters for the dashboard.

facts.claim: Cointelegraph (4 Jul 2025, citing SlowMist) reported that the GitHub repo solana-pumpfun-bot by account 'zldp2002' depended on crypto-layout-utils. That package had already been removed from npm and was being downloaded from a separate GitHub repo. It scanned local files and uploaded wallet data or private keys. Some forked repos used another malicious package, bs58-encrypt-utils-1.0.3 (created 12 June). The attacker likely controlled a batch of accounts that forked the repo to inflate stars and forks. Kaspersky GitVenom (24 Feb 2025) found hundreds of fake repos, including a 'Telegram bot allowing to manage Bitcoin wallets', delivering stealers, RATs and a clipboard hijacker. One attacker BTC wallet received about 5 BTC in Nov 2024.
facts.as_of: 2025-02-24 / 2025-07-04 (SlowMist primary at slowmist.medium.com was blocked by Cloudflare)
facts.design_relevance: No third-party 'sniper bot' code should be run on a machine with keys, and star or fork counts are not evidence of safety. The build should vendor only reviewed, pinned code.
facts.original_claim: Cointelegraph (4 Jul 2025, citing SlowMist) reported that the GitHub repo 'solana-pumpfun-bot' by account 'zldp2002' depended on the obfuscated npm package crypto-layout-utils, along with bs58-encrypt-utils-1.0.3. The package scanned local files for wallet data or private keys and uploaded them. The attacker used a batch of accounts to fork the repo and inflate stars and forks. Kaspersky's GitVenom report (24 Feb 2025) found hundreds of fake GitHub projects, including a 'Telegram bot... to manage Bitcoin wallets', that delivered stealers and a clipboard address-replacer; one attacker wallet received about 5 BTC in Nov 2024.
facts.note: bs58-encrypt-utils-1.0.3 appeared in forked repos, not 'along with' crypto-layout-utils in the original repo. Everything else matches. The SlowMist primary source was not checked.

facts.claim: The Anza Solana CLI docs say 'File system wallets are the least secure method of storing SOL tokens. Storing large amounts of tokens in a file system wallet is not recommended.' The keypair file is unencrypted JSON, and a password, if given, applies to the recovery seed phrase, not the file.
facts.design_relevance: If the hot key is a keypair file, only a small capped balance should sit there. The treasury should use a separate key held offline or in hardware, and the key file should be encrypted at rest and readable only by the signer process.
facts.note: The quotes match verbatim, including 'even if you specify a password, that password applies to the recovery seed phrase, not the file'.

facts.claim: AWS KMS supports key spec ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519 for signing only. Algorithm ED25519_SHA_512 requires MessageType RAW, and ED25519_PH_SHA_512 requires DIGEST. Sign accepts messages of 1-4096 bytes. Pricing is $1/month per key; the page's worked example prices ECC (P-256) signing at $0.15 per 10,000 requests, and asymmetric requests are excluded from the 20,000-request free tier.
facts.as_of: fetched 2026-10-06 (the Ed25519 per-request price is region-templated and did not render; the $0.15 figure is the P-256 example)
facts.design_relevance: AWS KMS can sign standard Solana Ed25519 messages, and Solana transactions fit within 4096 bytes. It costs about $1-2/month, but each signature adds a network round-trip, which conflicts with speed.
facts.note: ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519 is signing/verification only, with RAW for ED25519_SHA_512 and DIGEST for ED25519_PH_SHA_512. The Sign length constraint is min 1 and max 4096 (the prose says 0-4096). Keys cost $1/month. The $0.15/10k figure is the ECC 256 signing example, and asymmetric Sign is excluded from the 20k free tier. Per-request prices are region-templated.

facts.claim: Google Cloud KMS offers EC_SIGN_ED25519 (PureEdDSA over raw data) only at the SOFTWARE protection level. It is absent from the HSM, HSM-single-tenant, external and external-VPC tables (page updated 2026-09-30). Azure Key Vault lists only the P-256, P-256K, P-384 and P-521 EC curves, with no Ed25519 (page updated 2026-07-30).
facts.design_relevance: Google Cloud KMS supports Ed25519 only with software protection, not HSM, and Azure Key Vault does not support Ed25519 at all. The KMS branch therefore comes down to AWS KMS or GCP software keys.
facts.note: In the GCP EC tables, EC_SIGN_ED25519 appears in the 'software' table and is absent from the hsm, hsm-single-tenant, external and external-vpc tables (last updated 2026-09-30). The Azure EC curves are P-256, P-256K, P-384 and P-521 (updated 2026-07-30).

facts.claim: HashiCorp Vault's Transit engine supports key type 'ed25519' for signing, verification and key derivation; the docs note ed25519 is not certified in FIPS mode. The Yubico YubiHSM 2 (v2.4) is listed at $650 USD and supports 'EdDSA (curve25519 only)'.
facts.design_relevance: A hardware HSM at $650 is 65% of the bankroll and cannot be justified. A local signer process or Vault Transit gives key isolation without that cost.
facts.note: Vault supports ed25519 for signing, verification and key derivation, and states it is not certified in FIPS 140-3 mode (Enterprise). The YubiHSM 2 v2.4 is $650 USD with 'EdDSA (curve25519 only)'.

facts.claim: Solana's simulateTransaction RPC method does not require a signed transaction unless sigVerify is true. With replaceRecentBlockhash the node supplies the blockhash. The method can return chosen post-simulation account data ('accounts'), logs, unitsConsumed, innerInstructions, returnData and fee.
facts.design_relevance: Before entry, the bot can simulate a combined buy-then-sell transaction without signing and measure how much comes back. This catches hooks, fees and pauses active now, but not authorities used later, which is why authority checks stay mandatory.
facts.note: The page says 'not required to be signed unless sigVerify is true' and that the node replaces the blockhash when replaceRecentBlockhash is set. The config has accounts and innerInstructions, and the response has logs, unitsConsumed, returnData and fee.

facts.claim: Solana RPC docs say 'processed' is 'The node's most recent processed block... it can still be rolled back'. 'Confirmed' is a block voted on by more than two-thirds of active stake, and when commitment is omitted 'the default is typically finalized'.
facts.design_relevance: Authority and extension checks should be read at confirmed or stronger commitment, ideally cross-checked on a second RPC provider. A processed-only read can be rolled back.
facts.note: The processed, confirmed (more than two-thirds of stake) and 'default is typically finalized' quotes all match.

facts.topic: Trade journal fields for tax (examples, not advice)
facts.claim: The IRS says computing gain or loss requires the type of digital asset, date and time, number of units, fair market value in USD at the time, and basis (page reviewed 2026-09-02). The CRA lists the number of units and type, date and time, value in CAD at the time, the nature of the transaction and the other party ('even if it is just their crypto-asset address'), wallet addresses used, and beginning and ending wallet balances and cost for each year. CRA requires keeping records for at least 6 years (page modified 2025-11-10).
facts.design_relevance: These two examples suggest an append-only journal recording UTC time, signature and slot, mint and token program, raw units and decimals, fiat value at the time, all fees, pool or counterparty address, wallet address, and yearly opening and closing balances, kept for at least 6 years. Jurisdiction is unknown, so this is not tax advice.
facts.note: The IRS list matches (last reviewed 02-Sep-2026). The CRA list was fetched via WebFetch because curl failed. It includes units and type, date/time, CAD value, nature and other party including addresses, wallet addresses, and the beginning balance with its cost plus the ending balance. Records must be kept at least 6 years (modified 2025-11-10).

facts.claim: Cloudflare's Access product page describes its free plan as 'Best for teams under 50 users or enterprise proof-of-concept tests', with pay-as-you-go above that.
facts.design_relevance: The dashboard can sit behind an identity-aware proxy at no monthly cost, instead of being exposed directly on the internet.
facts.note: The page shows the Free Plan at '$0 forever', 'Best for teams under 50 users or enterprise proof-of-concept tests', and pay-as-you-go at $7/user/month.

facts.topic: Pump.fun Token-2022 mints: authorities after creation
facts.claim: Two fresh pump.fun ('...pump') mints read on 2026-10-06 via public RPC getAccountInfo (jsonParsed, commitment confirmed) were owned by TokenzQdBNbLqP5VEhdkAS6EPFLC1PHnBqCXEpPxuEb with decimals 6 and supply 1,000,000,000,000,000 base units (1B tokens). mintAuthority and freezeAuthority were null, and the only extensions were metadataPointer (authority null, pointing at the mint) and tokenMetadata (updateAuthority null). RugCheck reports for other '...pump' mints showed the same null authorities. This is an observation from samples, not a documented guarantee. Any '...pump' mint with a live mint, freeze, pointer or metadata authority, or any extra extension, deviates from the observed launchpad pattern.
facts.design_relevance: This partly answers the researcher's open question about the Pump PDA mint authority. It gives the token gate a concrete expected profile for ordinary pump.fun coins: all authorities null, and only MetadataPointer and TokenMetadata present.

facts.topic: Rug base rates are lower bounds (labeling window)
facts.claim: In arXiv 2603.24625 the labels use a 24-hour observation window. In a random sample of 100 tokens labelled non-rug, 9 were confirmed missed rugs that unfolded over 3-7 days. Freeze Authority Abuse is labelled only if a FreezeAccount was actually executed, so dormant but live freeze authorities do not count.
facts.design_relevance: The ~76% rate is a conservative lower bound and does not cover slow rugs. The 461 freeze cases undercount the latent risk of live freeze authorities. Time stops and re-checks must also cover multi-day holds.

facts.topic: RugCheck free insider and new-token endpoints
facts.claim: The RugCheck swagger lists GET /v1/tokens/{id}/insiders/graph, GET /v1/tokens/{id}/insiders/networks, GET /v1/stats/new_tokens and GET /v1/tokens/{id}/metadata with no security requirement. Only the lockers, bulk, verify and POST endpoints need the JWT Authorization key. new_tokens returned the mint, creator, mintAuthority, freezeAuthority, program and createAt for recent mints. Every response carried x-rate-limit-limit: 15.
facts.design_relevance: These provide a no-cost insider and cluster cross-check and a new-mint feed for the design, within an undocumented rate limit. The lockers endpoint, needed for LP-lock checks, is not free.

facts.topic: PumpSwap admin powers beyond the README
facts.claim: The current PumpSwap IDL (pump_amm.json) has admin instructions not described in the README, including admin_cto_pool, set_coin_creator, toggle_mayhem_mode and toggle_cashback_enabled. Its update_fee_config also takes coin_creator_fee_basis_points. The README says GlobalConfig.disable_flags is 'Currently, it is not used', which conflicts with the disable() instruction it also documents.
facts.design_relevance: The venue circuit breaker and cost model should read live GlobalConfig state (disable_flags and fee fields) on-chain, not trust the README. Venue fees, including creator fees, can be changed by the admin.

facts.claim: Official docs (solana.com/docs/tokens/extensions/permissioned-burn and the solana-program.com Token-2022 guide) document the PermissionedBurn extension and the CLI flag --permissioned-burn. They tell users to load 'the v11.0.0 program from devnet', which implies it is on devnet. The docs do not say whether it is on mainnet.
facts.design_relevance: The extension parser must handle this type now. Its mainnet availability should be checked against the deployed program before the allow/deny policy is finalised.

facts.claim: Marino, Naviglio, Tarantelli & Lillo, 'Predicting the success of new crypto-tokens: the Pump.fun case' (arXiv:2602.14860, 16 Feb 2026): over 1 Sep to 1 Oct 2025, 655,770 new pump.fun tokens and 2,600,790 distinct trader addresses; 4,338 tokens graduated, about 0.63%. Graduated tokens took a median of about 4.4 minutes and about 457 trades to graduate.
facts.design_relevance: Base rate for strategy (a)/(b): more than 99% of launches never graduate. Success is decided within minutes, so any graduation-prediction signal must be computed and acted on at slot/second latency.
facts.note: Abstract page lists Marino, Naviglio, Tarantelli, Lillo; v1 is dated 16 Feb 2026. The text gives 1 Sep to 1 Oct 2025, 655,770 tokens, 2,600,790 distinct traders, 4,338 graduated (about 0.63%), a median of about 4.4 minutes, and a median of about 457 'steps'. The paper defines a step as one bonding-curve swap event.

facts.topic: Graduation play: buy-and-hold to graduation is below breakeven
facts.claim: The paper defines a naive buy-and-hold breakeven: buy when vSol first reaches the entry level, sell at graduation (vSol = 115), and lose 100% otherwise. Profit requires p(vSol) > vSol^2/115^2, and protocol, creator and gas fees are neglected. The paper says p_std(vSol) lies below this curve, 'hence it is not possible to make profits with a buy-and-hold strategy based only on vSol (or the price)'. The sentence 'all conditional graduation-probability curves remain below the economic breakeven over most of the vSol range, with the notable exception of the p0.3 curve' sits in the bot-share section, where p0.3 means at least 30% non-bot trades. The top-trader-conditioned curves are also stated to be below breakeven. The text of the trading-intensity section makes no breakeven comparison; it says fast-accumulation curves lie 'well above the baseline'. The authors add that dynamic strategies could still be profitable below this curve.
facts.design_relevance: Strong evidence against naive pre-graduation 'ride to migration' plays even before fees. Any graduation strategy must beat this breakeven curve after fees, with latency modelled.
facts.original_claim: Same paper (arXiv:2602.14860) tests buying when the bonding-curve virtual SOL (vSol) hits an entry level, holding to graduation (vSol = 115, i.e. 30 virtual + 85 real SOL), and losing 100% if the token never graduates. Fees and gas are ignored. Profit requires p(vSol) > vSol^2/115^2. The authors conclude 'it is not possible to make profits with a buy-and-hold strategy based only on vSol (or the price)'. Curves conditioned on trading intensity and on bot share stay 'below the economic breakeven over most of the vSol range'. The only exception is one bot-share curve (p0.3), which approaches breakeven near the threshold.
facts.note: The formula, the fee-neglect statement and the quotes are verified. The claim attaches the 'below breakeven' statement to the trading-intensity curves, which the text does not support; it belongs to the bot-share and top-trader curves.

facts.claim: isBot = 1 marks transactions that call the contract directly, bypassing the pump.fun website frontend. Tokens that reach a given vSol with fewer trades graduate more often, and the paper calls this 'the strongest predictor'. A 'large participation of non-sophisticated traders is associated with an increased likelihood of reaching graduation'. The paper gives no single aggregate bot share, but it does give aggregate information: Fig. 6 (bottom) plots the mean bot rate against price level, and the text says 'the average non-bot rate in our data lies between' 0.3 and 0.7.
facts.design_relevance: Candidate features for a graduation model: accumulation speed and direct-call share. The 'isBot' proxy is crude, because terminals also call the contract directly, so any feature built on it needs validation.
facts.original_claim: arXiv:2602.14860 flags trades as bot trades (isBot=1) when they call the contract directly rather than going through the pump.fun website. Tokens that reach a given vSol level with fewer trades (fast accumulation) graduate much more often. A 'large participation of non-sophisticated traders is associated with an increased likelihood of reaching graduation'. The paper gives no aggregate bot share of trades.
facts.note: The definition and both findings are verified. The statement that the paper gives no aggregate bot share is too strong.

facts.claim: Of 184,282 tokens with at least 30 swaps, 169,938 (92.22%) show at least one dump event. A dump is the first log-return below -k*sigma_MAD with k = 4, using a median/MAD Shewhart rule. Only 2.55% of those 184,282 tokens graduate. The authors interpret the pattern as creators or tightly connected early wallets offloading inventory, often before graduation, once enough SOL has accumulated.
facts.design_relevance: Pre-graduation positions face near-certain insider selling. The risk engine needs creator/early-wallet sell detection and very tight exit rules.
facts.original_claim: arXiv:2602.14860: of 169,938 analyzable tokens, 92.22% show at least one dump event (first log-return breaching a 4-sigma robust MAD lower limit). The authors describe creators or tightly connected early wallets offloading inventory, often before graduation, once enough SOL has accumulated.
facts.note: The claim wrongly gives 169,938 as the denominator. 169,938 is the number of tokens with dumps; the analysed sample is 184,282.

facts.claim: The Block (James Hunt, 27 Feb 2025), citing its data dashboard, says the graduation rate peaked at 2.1% in June 2024. It was 1.6% 'by the time daily token launches and trading volumes had peaked', around late January 2025, not a stated January monthly rate. It was near an all-time low of 0.7% earlier in the week of publication. 24,008 tokens graduated to Raydium in January 2025. Solana Compass (10 Jun 2026) reports about 42,000 launches in one day and 11.9M launches in total, says 'fewer than 2%' ever graduate (citing The Block), and says Dune dashboards put the historical rate at about 1.4%.
facts.design_relevance: Base rates move a lot with regime (2.1% down to 0.6-0.7%). Backtests must be split by period and must not assume a stationary base rate.
facts.original_claim: The Block (27 Feb 2025), citing its own data dashboard and Dune: the graduation rate peaked at 2.1% in June 2024, was 1.6% in January 2025 (24,008 tokens graduated that month) and about 0.7% in early February 2025. Solana Compass (10 Jun 2026) reports about 42,000 launches in one day, about 11.9M launches in total, and a historical Dune-based graduation rate of about 1.4%.
facts.note: The numbers are verified. The 1.6% figure is tied to the late-January peak, not to the January month as a whole.

facts.claim: Crypto Briefing, which embeds pump.fun's X post of 21 Jul 2026, says all eligible coins migrating after 10:23 a.m. ET on 21 July automatically use BOOST. Coins launched through the Mayhem system are excluded. In the 5 minutes after migration BOOST re-injects 17.6 SOL (SOL pairs) or $2,516 (USDC pairs) through time-weighted purchases, and the tokens bought are burned after each transaction. The Block (29 Jul 2026; Ivan Wu and Bryan Samsoedin) reports a 6.7% single-day graduation rate, about 8x the June average, and a 4.7% four-day average against 2.5% the week before. It names no dashboard and says BOOST 'operates entirely after a token has already bonded, so it doesn't mechanically lift the share of tokens that reach the threshold'.
facts.design_relevance: Structural break: post-migration studies from before 21 Jul 2026 (including ST-10/ST-11) may not describe current dynamics. The backtester needs explicit regime boundaries, and live validation must use post-BOOST data.
facts.original_claim: Crypto Briefing (21 Jul 2026), citing pump.fun's official X post: from 10:23 a.m. ET on 21 Jul 2026, 'BOOST' is the default for new pump.fun coins. On migration it re-injects 17.6 SOL (SOL pairs) or $2,516 (USDC pairs) as TWAP market buys over 5 minutes and burns the tokens bought. The Block (29 Jul 2026) reports the graduation rate hit 6.7% on one day, about 8x the June average, with a 4.7% four-day average against 2.5% the week before. The Block gives no dashboard URL and notes BOOST does not mechanically change the bonding threshold.
facts.note: Eligibility is keyed to the migration time, not to new coin creation, and Mayhem coins are excluded. The other numbers are verified. The Block page returns 403 to curl and was read with WebFetch.

facts.claim: Ding, Luo & Xu, 'Decompose Market Manipulation Strategies: Evidence from On-chain Meme Coin Market' (SBFC 2025 paper): a stratified, weighted sample of 6,000 pump.fun projects (3,000 before and 3,000 after 17 Jan 2025; Flipside data). Sniper bots, defined as buys within the first five blocks, appear in 84% of projects. Rat bots (creator-controlled wallets trading in the creation block) appear in 24%, wash-trading bots in 4% and comment bots in 26%. The median project has 9 participants, and its median maximum return is about 15% (median ln max return 0.14).
facts.design_relevance: Launch sniping is saturated: most launches already have bots buying in blocks 0-4. A late sniper buys after them, at higher prices on the bonding curve.
facts.note: Authors are Ding, Luo and Xu. The sample is 6,000 projects: 3,000 before and 3,000 after the 17 Jan 2025 $TRUMP launch, stratified and weighted, with Flipside data. Weighted shares: rat bots 24%, sniper bots 84% (first five blocks), wash-trading bots 4%, comment bots 26%. Median maximum return is about 15% (median ln 0.14) and the median project has 9 participants.

facts.claim: All of the claim holds except one detail. The -$6.37 average non-creator loss per project applies to projects without wash-trading bots. With wash-trading bots the loss is -$4.47 (= -$6.37 + $1.90).
facts.design_relevance: Robust losers outnumber robust winners about 4.6 to 1, and winners are disproportionately insiders or early snipers. A non-insider, non-colocated bot starts on the losing side unless it proves otherwise.
facts.original_claim: Same SBFC 2025 paper: 4,000 single-wallet traders were sampled, keeping those active in more than 2 and fewer than 1,000 projects (algorithmic traders excluded). Of 2,448 in Table 6 (2,459 in the text), 182 were 'winners' (per-trader return t-stat > 2.65), 1,436 'normal' and 830 'losers' (t < -2.65). 19.2% of winners had created coins and 16.0% had used sniper bots; among losers the figures were 0.8% and 1.0%. Creators were the most frequent dumpers (about half of cases). Sniper presence cut creator profit by about $54. Average non-creator loss was -$6.37 per project.
facts.note: Verified: 4,000 single-wallet traders sampled; 2,459 in the text against 182 + 1,436 + 830 = 2,448 in Table 6; t = ±2.65; winners 19.2% creators and 16.0% snipers (35/182 and 29/182); losers 0.8% and 1.0%; creators dump in about half of cases; snipers cut creator profit by $54.

facts.claim: Hu, Tekin, Xu & Liu, 'MELT: A Behavioral Trace Dataset for High-Risk Memecoin Launch Detection' (arXiv:2602.13480v2, 21 May 2026): over 41,470 migrated pump.fun memecoins (1 Dec 2024 to 1 Mar 2025), '98.7% of create events co-occur with developer buys in the same transaction'. Bundled or coordinated accounts held 28.13% of holders and 36.50% of total token supply at migration.
facts.design_relevance: No outside sniper can get the first price tier: it goes to the developer atomically with creation. The first buys an outside bot can land are already behind insider inventory.
facts.note: v2 is dated 21 May 2026, by Hu, Tekin, Xu and Liu. The data runs 1 Dec 2024 to 1 Mar 2025 and covers 41,470 coins. The paper says '98.7% of "create" events co-occur with developer buys in the same transaction', and Table 3 'All' gives a bundled holder share of 28.13% and a bundled supply share of 36.50%.

facts.claim: MELT (arXiv:2602.13480v2): 'about 73% of memecoins drop below 40% of their migration price' within 20 minutes after migration (min_price_ratio = minimum price in the window / migration price). 84.13% (34,890) of the 41,470 migrated coins were labelled high-risk (min_price_ratio < 0.3 or manipulated), 11.34% medium and 4.53% low (min_price_ratio >= 0.7 and not manipulated).
facts.design_relevance: Migration is usually an insider exit event. Strategy (b) 'buy the graduation' and (c) breakout entries in the first ~20 minutes face severe adverse selection.
facts.note: With y = 20 minutes, 'about 73% of memecoins drop below 40% of their migration price'. High-risk means min_price_ratio < 0.3 or manipulated; low-risk means min_price_ratio >= 0.7 and not manipulated. The split is 84.13% (34,890) high, 11.34% medium and 4.53% low.

facts.claim: MELT (arXiv:2602.13480v2): buying top-k tokens at the migration price and selling at 100 random times within the next hour gives average losses above 60% with random selection. The best risk model (MLP) reduces losses to about 30%. Absolute returns are negative for every approach tested.
facts.design_relevance: Even a good risk filter only reduced losses. Good risk classification is not the same as a profitable entry signal.
facts.note: In Table 10, buying at the migration price and selling at 100 random times within the next hour gives a 60.71% loss (top-100) and 64.84% (top-200) without a model. MLP is best at 26.64% and 31.47%. All approaches lose money.

facts.claim: Pine Analytics, 'Exit Liquidity Machines' (21 Apr 2025, Flipside dashboards plus Arkham): in one month, deployer-funded sniping realized more than 15,000 SOL of profit across 15,000+ launches (about 1.75% of pump.fun launch activity), 4,600+ sniper wallets and 10,400+ deployers. 87% of snipes were profitable, 55% fully exited in under one minute and 85% within five minutes.
facts.design_relevance: The documented high-win-rate sniping is insider, creator-funded activity, which is out of bounds (bundled self-launch). It is not evidence that third-party sniping is profitable. Detecting it is a defensive feature (owned by TH).
facts.note: Pine Analytics, 21 Apr 2025, sources linked to Flipside dashboards and Arkham. Over the past month: more than 15,000 SOL of realized profit, 15,000+ launches, 4,600+ sniper wallets, 10,400+ deployers, about 1.75% of launch activity, 87% of snipes profitable, more than 55% fully exited in under 1 minute and about 85% within 5 minutes. The snipes are deployer-funded and same-block. This is a Substack analytics post, not peer-reviewed.

facts.claim: Luo, Feng, Xu & Liu (WWW '26; v2 26 Jan 2026, superseded by v3 on 5 Feb 2026) used 6,000 pump.fun coins with Flipside data. Train/validation/test is a 70/15/15 split, ordered chronologically by each trader's first transaction in a coin. The v2 abstract reports a 14% average return for identified smart-money trades and an estimated copier return of 3% per trade. The v3 abstract gives only 'an average copier return of 3% per meme coin investment'. The copier model (Appendix A.6) assumes one-to-one immediate replication: the copier trades the same quantity right after each smart-money trade on the bonding curve and pays the 1% pump.fun fee. It is not a later-block or latency model. Even this best case overpays on every buy by a factor of Y/(Y-2d). Statistic-driven selectors (LASSO, XGBoost, NN) produced positive smart-money returns but negative copier returns. No statement was found that the method was untested in live deployment.
facts.design_relevance: Even a favourable academic simulation loses about 79% of the leader's edge to the copier. Plain statistical wallet ranking went negative. Copy-trading must be validated with an explicit detection-to-landing latency model.
facts.original_claim: Luo, Feng, Xu & Liu, 'Resisting Manipulative Bots in Meme Coin Copy Trading: A Multi-Agent Approach with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning' (arXiv:2601.08641v2, WWW '26): on 6,000 pump.fun meme coins with a chronological 70/15/15 split, selected smart-money trades averaged 14% return, but the estimated copier return was 3% per trade. The copier model buys in later blocks on the bonding curve, pays a 1% fee and exits when the leader exits. Statistic-driven selectors (LASSO, XGBoost, NN) produced negative copier returns despite identifying profitable leaders. The authors note copier returns assume synchronized execution and that the method was not tested in live deployment.
facts.note: The key correction is the copier model: immediate, zero-intervening-trade replication, not later blocks. Real copiers with latency face extra adverse movement, so the 3% is an upper-bound-style estimate. The 'not tested in live deployment' caveat is not in v2 or v3 as read. v3 is the current version.

facts.claim: The paper describes bundle bots, gradual bundles, sniper bots (purchases 'typically within the first one to five blocks', about 0.4 to 2 s), bump bots (repeated buy/sell of identical quantities) and comment bots. The adversary aims to 'acquire meme coins at very early stages', and the paper models adversary and copiers as 'a near zero-sum game': 'the adversary's profits come directly from the losses of copy traders'. The quoted phrase 'leaving the copier with a loss' was not found in v2 or v3.
facts.design_relevance: Leader wallets can be bait. Wallet selection needs anti-manipulation filters and out-of-sample leader performance, not past PnL alone.
facts.original_claim: arXiv:2601.08641 lists bot types that extract value from copiers: bundle bots, sniper bots (purchases 'within the first one to five blocks'), bump bots (repeated equal-size buy/sell), comment bots and 'gradual bundles'. Adversaries 'acquire meme coins at very early stages' and exit, 'leaving the copier with a loss'.
facts.note: The substance is verified, but one quoted phrase is not verbatim in the text read.

facts.claim: Personal blog (article:published_time 2025-12-20; no code or data link found). It simulates 100,000 copy-trading attempts following the top 50 leader wallets. The dataset is described both as a 24-hour sample (1,428,590 trades, 5,842 tokens) and as 'representative days in 2025 and early 2026', which conflicts with the December 2025 publication date. In the table, 5 SOL is the LEADER's trade size, not the copier's. Slippage is 2.54% at 0.5 s and 24.12% at 5.0 s. Win rate is 46% at 0.5 s, 28% at 1.0 s and 4% at 5.0 s, and the post says copying is 'a mathematically guaranteed losing strategy' at latency >= 2.0 s.
facts.design_relevance: Directionally consistent with ST-13: copy-trading edge collapses within seconds. Treat only as a hypothesis for the bot's own latency-sweep backtest.
facts.original_claim: Personal blog by R. Kurnovskii (20 Dec 2025; no code or data published) simulated following the top 50 pump.fun leader wallets over a 24h sample (1,428,590 trades, 5,842 tokens). For a 5 SOL trade, slippage was 2.54% at 0.5 s latency and 24.12% at 5.0 s. Win rate was 46% at 0.5 s, 28% at 1.0 s and 4% at 5.0 s, and the strategy is called a 'guaranteed losing strategy' at latency >= 2.0 s.
facts.note: The numbers match, but the 5 SOL row is the leader trade size and the post's dates conflict internally. This is very weak evidence.

facts.claim: Decrypt (10 Jan 2025), citing Dune queries by analyst Adam Tehc: of over 13.4M pump.fun wallets, 55,012 (0.412%) had realized more than $10,000 and 294 (about 0.002%) more than $1M. The data excludes buys after graduation but includes post-graduation sells.
facts.design_relevance: Large realized wins are extremely rare. The design must not assume right-tail outcomes are reachable.
facts.note: Decrypt (Ryan S. Gladwin, 10 Jan 2025) citing Adam Tehc: 55,012 of over 13.4M wallets (0.4%; the tweet says top 0.412%) realized at least $10,000, and 294 wallets (about 0.002%) realized more than $1M. The data excludes buys after graduation but includes sells after graduation. The article also quotes '289' millionaires, and Tehc concedes that bots, including bump bots, skew the figures.

facts.claim: CoinGecko Research (7 May 2026; Dune dashboard coingecko_content/pump-fun-annual-trader-profitability) measures realized PnL only, netted per wallet, with bots and wash trading not filtered, and says the method 'understates losses'. April 2026 tiers: 65.1% gained $1-500, 2.8% gained $500-1K, 5.4% gained $1K+, 25.2% lost $1-500. Monthly active wallets fell from 5.2M (May 2025) to 1.8M (Dec 2025).
facts.design_relevance: Profitability metrics are non-stationary and depend on method: realized-only figures exclude bagholders. They cannot be compared with ST-16 and do not show after-cost edge for any strategy.

Profitable share: 47.58%, 30.08%, 56.83%, 73.28%. April 2026 tiers: 65.14%, 2.77%, 5.37%; 25.23% lost $1-500 (0.71% lost $500-1K and 0.78% lost more than $1K).
