facts.note: Forklog (10.06.2025) embeds Adam Tehc's 9 June 2025 tweet: '93 out of the top 100 pumpfun/pumpswap wallets are bots', with only 'simple bot filtering' mentioned. The method is undisclosed; this is social-media-grade evidence.

facts.topic: Cross-chain meme coin outcomes and manipulation
facts.claim: Mongardini & Mei (v1 16 Apr 2025, v2 2 Jan 2026) collected 34,988 meme coins on Ethereum, BSC, Solana and Base. The price-performance shares are computed on the 20,327 tokens with updated price data, not on all 34,988, over mid-Oct 2024 to mid-Jan 2025. 31.79% kept exactly the same price and all of them recorded zero trading volume; 34.13% fell (median -27.97%) and 34.07% rose (median +21.46%). Of 707 tokens with gains above 100%, 82.8% showed evidence of manipulation (wash trading or Liquidity Pool-Based Price Inflation). Only 121 showed no manipulation or suspicious ownership; 80 of them were on Solana, a normalized success rate of 0.77%.
facts.design_relevance: Most big winners in the history used for backtests were manipulated. A momentum/breakout model trained on them learns to chase manipulation. Labels and features must account for wash trading.
facts.original_claim: Mongardini & Mei, 'A Midsummer Meme's Dream: Investigating Market Manipulations in the Meme Coin Ecosystem' (arXiv:2507.01963v2, posted 2 Jan 2026): 34,988 meme coins on Ethereum, BSC, Solana and Base, mid-Oct 2024 to mid-Jan 2025. 31.79% had zero trading volume, 34.13% fell (median -27.97%) and 34.07% rose (median +21.46%). Of the 707 tokens that gained more than 100%, 82.8% showed artificial growth or suspicious ownership concentration, and only 121 (17.1%) had no manipulation indicators. The normalized high-performer rate on Solana was 0.77%.
facts.note: The denominator for the percentage split is 20,327, not 34,988. Everything else is verified.

facts.topic: Scale of rug/pump-and-dump (vendor report via news)
facts.claim: Forklog (08.05.2025) reports Solidus Labs' 2025 Rug Pull Report: 98.6% of pump.fun memecoins are associated with rug pulls or pump-and-dumps. The embedded Solidus tweet itself says 98.7%. By January 2025 more than 7M coins had launched, and only about 97,000 kept liquidity of at least $1,000. 93% of 388,000 Raydium pools 'exhibited characteristics of rug pulls' (Forklog does not say 'soft rug'). Forklog calls $2,832 the 'average' damage, with 25% of cases at $732 and a maximum of $1.9M. The primary report was not read.
facts.design_relevance: Confirms that the backtest universe is overwhelmingly dead or scam tokens, so leaving them out creates extreme survivorship bias. Methodology was not reviewed (vendor surveillance firm).
facts.original_claim: Forklog (8 May 2025), reporting Solidus Labs' '2025 Rug Pull Report': 98.6% of pump.fun tokens are associated with rug pulls or pump-and-dumps. Of 7M+ tokens launched, only about 97,000 kept liquidity of at least $1,000. 93% of 388,000 Raydium pools showed soft-rug characteristics. The damage figure of $2,832 is reported as 'average' by Forklog but 'median' by other outlets, a conflict not resolved.
facts.note: Forklog's text and the Solidus tweet it embeds disagree (98.6% vs 98.7%). This is vendor research seen through a news outlet.

facts.claim: Cointelegraph (30 Jul 2024), citing pseudonymous 'Flip Research' on Raydium pools: one pool with $3 of liquidity showed more than $5M of 24h volume, and one project generated $10.8M of volume from $48 of liquidity with 2,845 wallets wash trading.
facts.design_relevance: Reported volume is not a reliable liquidity or interest filter. Filters should use pool reserves, unique independent funders and net flow, not raw volume.
facts.note: Cointelegraph, 30 Jul 2024, citing pseudonymous Flip Research: the FLOG-SOL pool had $3 of liquidity and more than $5M of 24h volume. One project had $10.8M of volume from $48 of liquidity, with 2,845 unique wallets wash trading to generate $28,000 in fees.

facts.claim: Helius 'Solana MEV Report' (Lostin, 15 Jan 2025) attributes the figures to ONE sandwich program (the 'Vpe' program), which Jito internal data says accounts for 'just under half of all Solana sandwich attacks'. They are not network-wide totals. Over 7 Dec to 5 Jan that program executed 1.55M sandwich transactions (about 51,600 per day) with 88.9% success and 65,880 SOL of profit (about 2,200 SOL per day), and paid 22,760 SOL in Jito tips. Memecoin traders are 'especially susceptible' because they 'set high slippage tolerances'. Reverted transactions peaked at 75.7% of non-vote transactions in April 2024.
facts.design_relevance: Backtests must model adverse execution (sandwich loss up to the slippage bound) and failed-transaction costs, not mid-price fills. Execution protection is owned by EX.
facts.original_claim: Helius 'Solana MEV Report' (published 15 Jan 2025; vendor research citing Jito data): 1.55M sandwich transactions over 30 days (7 Dec 2024 to 5 Jan 2025) with 88.9% success, about 51,600 per day and about 2,200 SOL per day of profit. Memecoin traders are particularly vulnerable because of 'high slippage tolerances'. Reverted transactions peaked at 75.7% of non-vote transactions in April 2024.
facts.note: The claim presents single-program statistics as the whole-network sandwich environment. Network-wide sandwich volume would be roughly double, but that is an inference.

facts.topic: Latency levers for a non-staked sender
facts.claim: Chorus One (validator operator; conflict of interest), 3 Dec 2024. Data comes only from Chorus One's own leader slots, 18-25 Nov 2024. 'The size of the priority fee generally doesn't influence a transaction's time to inclusion', and Jito 'tip size doesn't significantly impact the time to inclusion'. Stake-weighted QoS was most effective, with about 30% of 'slow' transactions included in under 13 s, against about 10% for Jito.
facts.design_relevance: Paying more does not reliably buy speed. Latency races are won by infrastructure (staked connections, co-location), which a <$1k bot cannot justify. Supports avoiding slot-race strategies.
facts.note: Chorus One, 3 Dec 2024, using only slots led by its main identity from 18 to 25 Nov 2024. Quotes: 'The size of the priority fee generally doesn't influence a transaction's time to inclusion'; 'tip size doesn't significantly impact the time to inclusion'. The page says both 30% and, later, '25%' for swQoS 'slow' users included within 13 s, an internal inconsistency; Jito is 10%. The author is a validator operator with a conflict of interest.

facts.claim: Kamat, 'Auditing Collector-Generated Graduation Labels on Pump.fun: Measurement Error and Temporal Non-Generalization' (arXiv:2607.02823, v4 10 Sep 2026; single-author preprint): on 749,816 mints (12 May to 10 Jun 2026), a pre-registered graduation model scored AUROC 0.8594 in development but 0.4642 in validation (95% CI 0.4112-0.5196, which includes 0.5). Calibration slope was 0.013. 'Two pass, six fail, and one is not evaluable' of nine pre-registered checks. The collector's TIMEOUT label 'does not establish platform-side non-graduation'.
facts.design_relevance: A concrete case of a backtest-strong model failing out of time. The pipeline needs strict temporal holdouts, calibration checks and labels taken from on-chain completion events, not collector timeouts.
facts.note: Single author, Arati Uday Kamat; v4 dated 10 Sep 2026. 749,816 mints from 12 May to 10 Jun 2026. Development AUROC 0.8594; validation AUROC 0.4642 with 95% interval [0.4112, 0.5196]; calibration slope 0.013; 'two pass, six fail, and one is not evaluable'; the TIMEOUT label 'does not establish platform-side non-graduation'.

facts.claim: Kamat (v2 23 Sep 2026) compares two pipelines from one research programme that are configured for different purposes. One is a cohort-detection pipeline that flags coordinated early-buyer wallets; the other logs a trader-side observer's pre-trade filter rejections. Over a 17.5-day window, 623 cohort mints and 1,742 rejection mints overlapped in 5 (0.803% and 0.287%). The author concludes that 'Collector configuration, not only market behaviour, therefore shapes which tokens an on-chain study observes'.
facts.design_relevance: Ingestion filters silently create selection bias. The research dataset must record every create event from the program logs and publish coverage and reconciliation metrics before any backtest is trusted.
facts.original_claim: Kamat, 'Do Two On-Chain Observation Pipelines See the Same Tokens? Cross-Pipeline Coverage on the Solana pump.fun Launchpad' (arXiv:2609.18975, v2 23 Sep 2026): over a 17.5-day window, one pipeline logged 623 mints and another 1,742, with only 5 in common (0.803% and 0.287%). The author concludes 'collector configuration, not only market behaviour, therefore shapes which tokens an on-chain study observes'.
facts.note: The numbers and the quote are verified. The two pipelines are purpose-filtered outputs, not two general-purpose create-event collectors, so the near-disjoint overlap partly reflects their different filters.

facts.claim: Ammann, Burdorf, Liebi & Stöckl, 'Survivorship and Delisting Bias in Cryptocurrency Markets' (SSRN 4287573, 2022): on 3,904 cryptocurrencies (2014-2021), annualized survivorship-plus-delisting bias is 0.93% for value-weighted and 62.19% for equal-weighted portfolios. The size premium is overestimated by 50% in survival-conditioned samples. There is no evidence of a positive return relation with one-week momentum, beta or downside risk after controlling for the bias.
facts.design_relevance: Equal-weighted per-token strategies, which is what a meme bot runs, are most exposed. Dead tokens and delisting returns of -100% must be in the backtest.
facts.note: The abstract gives 3,904 cryptocurrencies over 2014-2021, an annualized bias of 0.93% value-weighted and 62.19% equal-weighted, and a size premium 'overestimated by 50% in a survival-conditioned sample'. It finds 'no evidence of a positive relationship between average returns, one-week momentum, market β, and downside risk'. Crossref confirms the authors.

facts.topic: Momentum vs reversal by size/liquidity (CEX-listed crypto)
facts.claim: Fičura, 'Impact of size and volume on cryptocurrency momentum and reversal' (FFA Working Papers 5.003, 2023): small, illiquid coins show weekly return reversal (t = -7.31) and large, liquid coins show weekly momentum (t = 2.33). Distance from the 1-week high predicts returns negatively for small coins (t = -9.03) and positively for large ones (t = 4.93). Kozlowski, Puleo & Zhou, 'Cryptocurrency return reversals' (Applied Economics Letters, 2020): 200 cryptocurrencies 2015-2019 show reversals at daily, weekly and monthly frequencies, 'most pronounced among smaller capitalization and less liquid cryptocurrencies'.
facts.design_relevance: Weak support for testing mean reversion (e) on smaller tokens and momentum only on the largest. Samples are CEX-listed coins, not Solana DEX memecoins, so transferability is unproven.
facts.note: Fičura (FFA WP 5.003, revised 5 Apr 2023): weekly reversal t = -7.31 and momentum t = 2.33; distance from the 1-week high t = -9.03 and t = 4.93. Kozlowski, Puleo & Zhou (Applied Economics Letters vol. 28, published 1 Jun 2020): 200 coins over 2015-2019, with reversals 'most pronounced among smaller capitalization and less liquid cryptocurrencies'.

facts.claim: Liu, Tsyvinski & Wu, 'Common Risk Factors in Cryptocurrency', Journal of Finance 77(2), 2022, pp. 1133-1177 (NBER WP 25882): cryptocurrency market, size and momentum factors capture cross-sectional expected crypto returns. This conflicts with ST-26, which finds no one-week momentum after survivorship adjustment.
facts.design_relevance: Evidence on momentum is mixed and depends on survivorship handling. Momentum/breakout (c) must be proven on a survivorship-complete Solana DEX dataset.
facts.note: The NBER page confirms market, size and momentum factors capture cross-sectional expected crypto returns, published as Journal of Finance 77(2), 2022, pp. 1133-1177. The stated conflict with ST-26 is the researcher's interpretation.

facts.claim: Bailey & López de Prado, 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality', Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5), 2014, pp. 94-107 (SSRN 2460551). DSR is a Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio whose rejection threshold is the expected maximum SR under the null. That threshold rises with the number of independent trials N and the variance of trial SRs, and it also uses sample length T and the selected strategy's skewness and kurtosis.
facts.design_relevance: The research harness must log every strategy/parameter trial (N, and the SR variance across trials) so DSR can be computed. A gate such as DSR >= 0.95 is a design choice built on this.
facts.note: Crossref gives JPM 40(5), 94-107, 2014; the PDF cites SSRN 2460551. DSR is a PSR whose threshold is the expected maximum SR, which grows with N and the variance of trial SRs. It also uses T and the selected strategy's skewness and kurtosis. The worked example shows N = 46 giving 0.9505.

facts.claim: Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu, 'The Probability of Backtest Overfitting', Journal of Computational Finance 20(4), Apr 2017, pp. 39-69 (DOI 10.21314/jcf.2016.322). PBO is 'the probability that the model configuration selected as optimal IS will underperform the median of the N model configurations OOS', estimated with combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV). The authors say 'a customary approach would be to reject models for which PBO is estimated to be greater than 0.05'.
facts.design_relevance: A concrete, citable promotion gate (PBO <= 0.05) for strategy selection. It needs a trials matrix (time x configurations) stored by the research harness.
facts.note: The escholarship PDF returned 403, so the authors' preprint was read instead. Bailey's list gives JCF vol. 20, no. 4 (Apr 2017), pp. 39-69, and Crossref confirms the DOI and authors. The PBO definition and the 'customary approach ... reject models for which PBO is estimated to be greater than 0.05' quote are verbatim.

facts.topic: Minimum backtest length vs number of trials
facts.claim: Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu, 'Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism: The Effects of Backtest Overfitting on Out-of-Sample Performance', Notices of the AMS, May 2014, pp. 458-471. MinBTL < 2 ln[N] / E[max_N]^2 years. 'if only 5 years of data are available, no more than 45 independent model configurations should be tried', otherwise in-sample SR of 1 is expected with out-of-sample SR of 0. For a 2-year backtest the limit is 7 configurations. MinBTL is 'a necessary, non-sufficient condition'.
facts.design_relevance: With only months of comparable meme-coin history per regime, the number of configurations the team may try is tiny. Parameter search must be budgeted and logged.
facts.note: Notices of the AMS, May 2014, pp. 458-471. The paper gives 'no more than 45 independent model configurations' for 5 years, 7 configurations for a 2-year backtest, and calls MinBTL 'a necessary, non-sufficient condition'.

facts.claim: Bailey & López de Prado, 'The Sharpe Ratio Efficient Frontier', Journal of Risk 15 (2012), pp. 3-44. The paper's own code computes MinTRL (in observations) = 1 + (1 - skew*SR + (kurt-1)/4*SR^2) * (Z_alpha/(SR - SR_ref))^2. Negative skew and fat tails lengthen it, and the authors caution the moments need samples beyond about 30 observations for the CLT to hold.
facts.design_relevance: Gives a formula for the minimum number of paper-trading or live trades before promotion, computed on per-trade returns with their actual skew and kurtosis.
facts.note: The paper's Python code computes minTRL = 1 + (1 - skew*sr + (kurt-1)/4*sr^2) * (norm.ppf(prob)/(sr - sr_ref))^2, where kurt is non-excess kurtosis. It notes the CLT is 'typically assumed to hold for samples in excess of 30 observations'. Crossref gives Journal of Risk 15(2), pp. 3-44.

facts.claim: Lo, 'The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios', Financial Analysts Journal 58(4), 2002, pp. 36-52: under IID returns SE(SR) ≈ sqrt((1 + SR^2/2)/T). Serial correlation can overstate an annual Sharpe ratio by 'as much as 65 percent'.
facts.design_relevance: Per-trade Sharpe from a few dozen trades has very wide error bars. Dashboards should show confidence intervals, not point estimates.
facts.note: Eq. 9 gives SE(SR) ≈ sqrt((1 + SR^2/2)/T), and the paper says the annual Sharpe ratio can be 'overstated by as much as 65 percent' because of serial correlation. FAJ 58(4), pp. 36-52. The IID formula does not account for fat tails.

facts.claim: Harvey, Liu & Zhu, '… and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns', Review of Financial Studies 29(1), 2016, pp. 5-68 (NBER w20592): accounting for multiple testing, 'a newly discovered factor needs to clear a much higher hurdle, with a t-ratio greater than 3.0'. Harvey & Liu, 'Backtesting', Journal of Portfolio Management 42(1), 2015, pp. 13-28, also verified as a citation.
facts.design_relevance: A simple secondary gate: the mean per-trade after-cost return t-stat must exceed 3, not 2, when many variants were tried.
facts.note: The quote 'a t-ratio greater than 3.0' is verified on the NBER page. RFS 29(1), pp. 5-68. Harvey & Liu, 'Backtesting', JPM 42(1), pp. 13-28, is confirmed via Crossref.

facts.topic: Data-snooping tests and bootstrap CIs (citations verified)
facts.claim: Citations verified via Crossref: White, 'A Reality Check for Data Snooping', Econometrica 68(5), 2000, pp. 1097-1126. Hansen, 'A Test for Superior Predictive Ability', JBES 23(4), 2005, pp. 365-380. Romano & Wolf, 'Stepwise Multiple Testing as Formalized Data Snooping', Econometrica 73(4), 2005, pp. 1237-1282. Politis & Romano, 'The Stationary Bootstrap', JASA 89(428), 1994, pp. 1303-1313. Bailey et al. (PBO paper) describe the White/Romano/Harvey methods as adjusting p-values 'to account for the multiplicity of trials'.
facts.design_relevance: Standard tests for 'is the best of many strategies really better than a no-trade benchmark'. A stationary/block bootstrap fits serially dependent trade sequences. Abstracts were not read in this session; only citations and secondary descriptions were checked.
facts.note: All four citations match Crossref exactly. The PBO preprint says 'See White [35], Romano et al. [27], Harvey et al. [13] ... adjust the p-values ... to account for the multiplicity of trials'. As the researcher said, only the citations are verified, not the content of each test.

facts.topic: Robust Sharpe comparison under heavy tails
facts.claim: Ledoit & Wolf, 'Robust performance hypothesis testing with the Sharpe ratio', Journal of Empirical Finance 15(5), 2008, pp. 850-859 (IEW WP 320, Jan 2008): the Jobson-Korkie/Memmel test 'is not valid when returns have tails heavier than the normal distribution or are of time series nature'. The authors propose 'a studentized time series bootstrap confidence interval for the difference of the Sharpe ratios'.
facts.design_relevance: Use for comparing a candidate strategy against baseline or no-trade on heavy-tailed meme returns, instead of normal-theory tests.
facts.note: Both quotes are verbatim. Journal of Empirical Finance 15(5), pp. 850-859.

facts.topic: Purged CV, embargo, walk-forward and CPCV
facts.claim: López de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning' (Wiley, published 21 Feb 2018, ISBN 978-1-119-48208-6). The Wiley table of contents includes 7.3 'Why K-Fold CV Fails in Finance', 7.4.1 'Purging the Training Set', 7.4.2 'Embargo', ch. 11 'The Dangers of Backtesting', ch. 12 'Backtesting through Cross-Validation' (Walk-Forward Method; Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation Method; 'Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation Addresses Backtest Overfitting') and ch. 14 'Backtest Statistics'.
facts.design_relevance: Defines the cross-validation scheme for ML-based filters. Labels overlap in time (holding windows), so purging and embargo are mandatory.
facts.note: The Wiley page shows ISBN 978-1-119-48208-6 and 'February 2018' but no day, so 21 Feb is not verified. The table of contents confirms 7.3, 7.4.1, 7.4.2, ch. 11, ch. 12 (12.2 Walk-Forward; 12.4 CPCV; 12.5 'How Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation Addresses Backtest Overfitting') and ch. 14 'Backtest Statistics'.

facts.topic: Kelly sizing: over-betting and fractional Kelly
facts.claim: MacLean, Thorp & Ziemba, 'Good and bad properties of the Kelly criterion' (1 Jan 2010). Kelly wagers 'may be very large' and are 'very risky in the short term'. Betting exactly 2x Kelly drives the growth rate to the risk-free rate in the continuous-time approximation. In their blackjack table (2% edge), Kelly fraction 0.5 gives P(double before halve) of 0.89 and relative growth of 0.75, and fraction 0.1 gives 0.999 and 0.19. Errors in means are about 20:2:1 in importance against variances and covariances. Given 'extreme sensitivity of E log calculations to errors in mean estimates … the size of the wagers should be reduced'.
facts.design_relevance: Sizing should use a small fraction of an estimated Kelly, haircut for estimation error in the mean edge. Overestimating the edge is the dominant ruin risk.
facts.note: Dated January 1, 2010. Quotes: 'may be very large', 'very risky in the short term', growth becomes 'zero plus the risk free rate when one bets exactly twice the Kelly wager' (continuous-time approximation), the 20:2:1 importance of errors, and 'the size of the wagers should be reduced'. The blackjack table (2% advantage) values 0.89/0.75 and 0.999/0.19 are consistent with the extracted table.

facts.claim: Same paper (MacLean, Thorp & Ziemba 2010): over 700 wagers each with a 14% advantage, full Kelly can turn $1,000 into $18. Half Kelly 'does not help much', since $1,000 can still become $145. It can take very long for a better strategy to dominate: with an edge of 1.0% against 1.1%, it takes 'two million trials to have an 84% chance' of telling them apart. Practitioners 'sharply reduce risk as their drawdown increases'.
facts.design_relevance: Even a genuine edge can produce deep drawdowns at small fractions. Supports drawdown-scaled sizing and hard daily/total loss caps independent of Kelly.
facts.note: Verbatim: 700 wagers at a 14% advantage can turn $1000 into $18; 'Half Kelly does not help much as $1000 can become $145'; edges of 1.0% vs 1.1% take 'two million trials to have an 84% chance'; practitioners 'sharply reduce risk as their drawdown increases'.

facts.claim: Busseti, Ryu & Boyd, 'Risk-Constrained Kelly Gambling' (arXiv:1603.06183, 20 Mar 2016) adds a bound on drawdown probability that turns the problem into a convex one with a single risk-aversion parameter. 'simulations show that this method yields bets that out perform fractional-Kelly bets' at comparable risk or growth.
facts.design_relevance: An alternative sizing method that targets drawdown probability directly. It needs the empirical outcome distribution per strategy, which paper trading must collect.

facts.topic: Copy-trading / wallet-following evidence on the bonding curve
facts.claim: Marino et al. pick top-PnL wallets from the first two weeks of Sep 2025 and condition on their early participation in the following two weeks, an ex-ante, out-of-sample signal. That signal raises the graduation probability above baseline, but the curves 'still are below the breakeven curve', and top traders 'tend to exit positions rapidly, often around ... graduation'. Several top-PnL wallets were sell-only, which suggests exit or aggregation wallets fed by other addresses.
facts.design_relevance: This is independent evidence that following wallets does not reach buy-and-hold breakeven even before fees. It also shows that ranking wallets by raw PnL selects aggregation or exit wallets, so the wallet selector needs cluster and transfer-graph filtering.

facts.topic: Mechanical copier penalty even at zero latency
facts.claim: Luo et al., Appendix A.6 and Lemma (v3): when a copier replicates the same quantity immediately after the leader on the bonding curve, each buy costs Y/(Y-2d) times what the leader paid (always more than 1), and each sell receives less. So R(copier) < R(leader) always, before any latency or intervening trades.
facts.design_relevance: The backtester's copier fill model must apply the leader's own price impact plus all trades between the leader's slot and the bot's landing slot. Filling at the leader's price overstates returns by construction.

facts.topic: Fee drag on bonding-curve strategies (as of Sep 2025 sample)

The paper's breakeven curve ignores these fees and gas, so the real breakeven is stricter, at roughly 2.5% round trip before priority fees and tips. The current fee schedule must be re-verified; it is UNVERIFIED for Oct 2026.
facts.design_relevance: Any graduation or snipe strategy test must subtract per-swap protocol and creator fees on both legs. The published breakeven is a lower bound, not an achievable target.

facts.topic: PumpSwap fee placement, rounding, market-cap input and schedule choice
facts.claim: Per the official @pump-fun/pump-swap-sdk 1.20.0, whose functions name the Rust code they mirror: each fee component is ceil(amount x bps / 10000), computed separately for lp, protocol and coin creator. Buy fees are added on top of the pre-fee quote input; sell fees are taken from the gross output. Buy exact quote in: q' = floor(quote x 10000 / (10000 + totalBps)), reduced if q' plus fees exceeds quote, and the swap input is q' - 1. Market cap for tier choice = floor(effective_quote x supply / base_reserve), with effective_quote = vault + virtual_quote_reserves, and supply fixed at 1e15 base units for mayhem pools. A tier applies when market cap >= threshold. Non-canonical pools pay flat_fees; canonical SOL-like quote (default key, wSOL, Token-2022 native) pays fee_tiers; canonical USDC pays stable_fee_tiers; other quotes pay exotic_flat_fees (flat_fees while exotic is all zero). The creator fee is 0 when Pool.coin_creator is the default key, and Pool.creator_fee_bps replaces the schedule's creator rate when GlobalConfig.creator_fee_configurable is true and creator_fee_bps > 0. Trade size does not affect the tier.
facts.design_relevance: Resolves U-A03 for A-M01-02/03 and A-M10-03; replaces SPEC-A's lower-of-two market-cap rule and adds the per-pool creator fee, mayhem supply and exotic schedule.
facts.note: SDK src/sdk/util.ts:8-17,37-60; buy.ts:71-113,184-240; sell.ts:69-112; fees.ts:68-108,125-183. The buy.ts comment says floor but the code uses ceilDiv.
